Q: Copy Date from Listbox and Paste into Textbox A:

CDate() is only "safe" if the text you pass to it is interpreted using the same regional settings you expect. For example CDate("03/04/2026") becomes 3 April 2026 on dd/MM systems and 4 March 2026 on MM/dd systems.

I would recommend checking if the value is numeric (Excel Date) and if not then try to parse it for dd/MM/yyyy. You can use this function.

Disclaimer: The below code is untested. I have commented the code. If you face any issue then simply leave a comment and I will take it from there.

Private Function IsItalianDate(ByVal LbDate As String, ByRef dt As Date) As Boolean
    On Error GoTo Whoa

    '~~> Remove leading and trailing spaces from the input
    LbDate = Trim$(LbDate)

    '~~> If the value is numeric, treat it as an Excel date serial
    If IsNumeric(LbDate) Then
        dt = CDate(CDbl(LbDate))   '<~~ Convert serial number to Date
        IsItalianDate = True
        Exit Function
    End If

    '~~> Split the string using Italian date separator "/"
    Dim parts() As String
    parts = Split(LbDate, "/")

    '~~> Italian date must have exactly 3 parts: dd, MM, yyyy
    If UBound(parts) <> 2 Then GoTo Whoa

    '~~> Extract day, month, and year explicitly
    Dim dd As Long, mm As Long, yy As Long
    dd = CLng(parts(0))   '<~~ Day
    mm = CLng(parts(1))   '<~~ Month
    yy = CLng(parts(2))   '<~~ Year

    '~~> DateSerial validates the date and raises an error if invalid
    dt = DateSerial(yy, mm, dd)

    '~~> If we reach here, parsing was successful
    IsItalianDate = True
    Exit Function

Whoa:
    '~~> Any error ends up here
    IsItalianDate = False
End Function

And then you can use it like this.

'
'~~> Rest of your code
'

Dim i As Long            '~~> Loop counter
Dim s As String          '~~> Raw value from ListBox
Dim dt As Date           '~~> Parsed Date value

'~~> Loop through all TextBox names stored in ArrTB
For i = LBound(ArrTB) To UBound(ArrTB)

    '~~> Read the value from the selected ListBox row and column
    s = CStr(Me.ListBox1.List(Me.ListBox1.ListIndex, i))

    '~~> Try to convert the value into a valid Italian date
    If IsItalianDate(s, dt) Then
        '~~> Write the date in dd/MM/yyyy format
        Me.Controls(ArrTB(i)).Value = Format$(dt, "dd/mm/yyyy")
    Else
        '~~> Clear TextBox if the value is not a valid date
        Me.Controls(ArrTB(i)).Value = ""
    End If

Next i

'
'~~> Rest of your code
'

Q: how to #define macro only to specific files? A:

File-by-File #define outside the File

What the OP was getting at, back in all those years, it is still a valid concern. But I think the real question here is how to define a macro for certain files, have a global value in effect, and not throw warnings or errors when you redefine a macro that is used in another header further down (read on for details on what this all means).

Per-File is Tedious and Can Only Be Done Two Ways

  1. By #define macro value in the start of the source file, guarded when its a header file.

  2. By using -Dmacro=value in the build command line for the file(s) in question. You would probably use makefile variables so you can change them more easily down the road. But this is quite tedious and requires a build system that is able to accommodate that. Many modern build systems use -D globally in all files during a build, and rarely support file-by-file command lines for build performance reasons.

If you want to do what OP is asking for, you would have to use a custom makefile with the -D flags set for each command line, appropriately:

g++ <other command line options> -Dmymacro=value myfile.cpp other-files-that-share-the-same-fate.cpp

TIP: If you use qmake, you can use DEFINES+= MACRO=value to add -D commands to your build inside your .pro project file.

However, unless the files you are compiling have a complex inclusion layout, it is generally best just to #define these in each file's header or source.

Global #define Issues: The Problem

Now, if you need a GLOBAL default value, and wish to only #define such a value only in certain files, it gets a bit trickier. People often mistakenly add a -DMYSYMBOL=defaultValue in their project and just re#define it when needed.

Overworking a Macro

While this sometimes works, doing so has drawbacks and can be destructive as you are trying to task one macro with two jobs which is more than it should have to handle:

  1. Provide a value for MACRO to the compiler

  2. Provide a default value for MACRO, this is not the same as providing an "initial value" as the compiler does not recognize any value as being an "initial state" or "default".

The compiler however, does not know you want to do #2 with MACRO, it simply sees whether or not it is defined. Consider:

  1. Most IDEs will -D macros globally, you would have to add it to your makefile for every step and file individually, which is a pain especially if you are using a build system that uses make or cmake dynamically. That is, the build tree is regenerated each time the project is built.

  2. The compiler normally sees -DMACRO=value as a #define MACRO=value at the beginning of each and every source file in the command line where -D is in effect.

  3. Because of the way -D works, it will throw redefinition warnings or errors just the same as if it had been typed. Additionally these warnings/errors are even more difficult to pinpoint in large projects and might lead you to the wrong conclusions while debugging your build.

To further explain, consider the following code:

/* header.h */
#ifndef MACRO
#define MACRO file_default
#endif
#define MYOTHERMACRO(text)  dosomething(MACRO)



/*  source1.cpp
use item from header above */
#ifdef MACRO  
#undef MACRO 
#endif
#define MACRO myfiletext /* will be used, no global -D define */
#include "header.h"
MYOTHERMACRO(that) // expands to "thatdosomething(myfiletext)"

/* source2.cpp */
/* when nothing gets #defined above in the source.cpp  */  
#include "header.h"
MYOTHERMACRO(that) // expands to thatdosomething(file_default)

/* source3.cpp */
/* when a command line parameter -DMACRO=override is present */
#include "header.h"
MYOTHERMACRO(that) // expands to thatdosomething(override)

/* source4.cpp */
/* when a command line parameter -DMACRO=override is present */
#include "header.h"
#define MACRO myvalue // would throw a warning, is defined!
MYOTHERMACRO(that) // still expands to thatdosomething(override) because of -D

In these files we are defining a macro value named MACRO. This macro is then used in a function-style macro named MYOTHERMACRO.

The problem arises when you start defining MACRO globally using the -DMACRO=value which applies to your global project unless you are setting it for every command line in your own Makefile.

source1.cpp: As you can see, the first use case uses our defined macro, because no -DMACRO=value has been defined globally. This generates no warnings or errors.

source2.cpp: In the second case, we didn't define MACRO, nor is it a -DMACRO=value, so file_default is used.

source3.cpp: In the third case, we didn't define MACRO, but -DMACRO=override is used, which is also seen the other header file.

source4.cpp: if we are using a global define, we'll get a warning in such cases as it is already defined globally. We could add guards, but the used value in the header would still be 'override'.

The Real Solution

To fix the problem, you need to have it so each macro is not taking on more than one job (as said above). This means you need to define globally (with -D) a second macro value to hold the DEFAULT value when one is not present, instead of expecting your MACRO to also contain the default value. Just like you wouldn't expect a template document to continue to hold your actual document, you shouldn't expect your MACRO to continue to hold a default value:

/* In all cases below, -DGLOBALDEFAULT=notdefined, is in effect */

/* header.h */

#ifndef MACRO
#define MACRO GLOBALDEFAULT
#endif

#define MYOTHERMACRO(text) text##dosomething(MACRO)

/* source1.cpp */
#define MACRO MYVALUE
#include "header.h"
MYOTHERMACRO(notdefault) /* expands notdefaultdosomething(MYVALUE) */

/* source2.cpp */
#include "header.h"
MYOTHERMACRO(notdefault) /* expands to notdefaultdosomething(GLOBALDEFAULT) */

This way, if there is no MACRO defined, the GLOBALDEFAULT will get used. This ensures MACRO does not get written into before the compiler knows whether or not to do so. It also allows you to avoid redefinition warnings or errors.

Footnotes:

  1. YMMV: Not all build systems handle command lines and techniques given above the same way. You may have to tweak the above code to work for you as intended.

  2. This code is pseudocode, and is meant only for demonstrating the concept, not for actual use in a project.

  3. Your build system might have facilities to do this without a second macro. If that is the case, you can use it. But it is generally more portable to involve the build tools as little as possible within the code.

  4. Avoid #define constants as much as possible. You should only use them as a last resort or when the situation cannot be resolved any other way. For constants, look into constexpr. Also check out lambdas and templates which may be more suited to the job. There are plenty of HOWTOs for these out there already.

  5. Personally, I only like using macros when I need to generate a lot of symbol names that may change that cannot be generated in any other way. Or, for generating important prefixes on symbols such as the current class name, or other API-related usage where I cannot use templates, lambdas, or constexpr.
